L2: ## About BluePearl Science.
L3: 
L4: Founded by our dedicated clinicians, BluePearl Science coordinates clinical studies to increase medical knowledge, advance veterinary practice and develop new diagnostic and treatment approaches that offer novel and potentially lifesaving options for pets.
L5: 
L6: 【1†Image: Pictured Jaime Rechy Jr, DVM, DACVR】
L7: 
L8: 【2†Watch on YouTube†www.youtube.com】
L9: 
L10: ## Our goals.
L11: ### Creating a better future for pets.
L12: 
L13: Innovative diagnostic and treatment solutions and pharmaceuticals can save pets' lives.
L14: 
L15: Assessing the effectiveness of drugs, diagnostics and procedures through clinical studies can help protect and promote the lives of pets today and tomorrow.
L16: 
L17: 【3†Image: ...】
L18: ### Sharing knowledge and expertise with the community.
L19: 
L20: We believe veterinarians can make the greatest impact when we work together.
L21: 
L22: Performing clinical studies to gain knowledge about new medical treatment options is part of our service to the national veterinary community. Data from these studies are published in peer-reviewed literature, allowing everyone to benefit from the findings.
L23: 
L24: 【4†Image: Veterinary Ophthalmologist Surgery】
L25: ### Coordinating with primary care veterinarians.
L26: 
L27: Our emergency and specialty clinicians share a common goal with primary care veterinarians: To provide exceptional care for your pet.
L28: 
L29: When your pet is involved in a clinical study at BluePearl, we will always keep your family veterinarian informed when it comes to diagnostic and treatment plans.
L30: 
L31: 【5†Image: Maia Derm Reiter】
L32: ### Collaborating with pet families.
L33: 
L34: Pets benefit from novel diagnostic or therapeutic options as part of BluePearl's clinical studies program and pet families are involved in every care decision along the way.
L35: 
L36: In all cases, both traditional and investigational treatments will be discussed so pet families can make informed care decisions for their specific circumstances.
L37: 【6†Image: Tina Fargo, an ophthalmology tech in the Tampa hospital, receives a kiss from patient Louie. Louie is an English Bulldog who had entropion eye surgery.】
L38: 
L39: 【7†Image: 】
L40: ## Frequently asked questions.
L41: 
L42: What is a clinical study?
L43: 
L44: Clinical studies are an important way of increasing medical knowledge, advancing veterinary practice and improving animal health.
L45: 
L46: Clinical studies at our hospitals can be sponsored by veterinarians or granting agencies seeking new ways to diagnose and treat disease in veterinary patients, by other groups within the Mars Petcare Ecosystem, and by pharmaceutical and technology companies developing new approaches to improve pet care.
L47: What benefits do clinical studies offer me and my pet?
L48: 
L49: By voluntarily participating in a clinical study, your pet may get access to new approaches to diagnosis and treatment of their condition not available outside the clinical studies setting. Participating in clinical studies also helps provide information that can benefit future pets with similar conditions.
L50: The best interests of the pet, the desires of the pet’s owner, and the mutually agreed upon course of treatment between the owner and veterinarian set the standard of care for both routine veterinary treatment and clinical studies at BluePearl Hospitals.
L51: 
L52: No pet is ever enrolled in a clinical study at BluePearl without the owner’s fully informed and written consent.
L53: 
L54: Can healthy pets participate in clinical studies?
L55: For some clinical studies, healthy animals might be able to participate, particularly when there is a need to compare information about healthy pets to pets with a particular disease.
L56: 
L57: When healthy pets are involved, study activities are non-invasive and might include things like bloodwork or observational assessments (those that just involve looking at the pet).
L58: 
L59: The Mars Petcare Biobank is an important example of how healthy pets can make a substantial difference in veterinary healthcare studies.
L60: How can my pet become involved?
L61: 
L62: If you believe that your pet may benefit from enrollment in a clinical study, please contact your family veterinarian.
L63: 
L64: Below is a complete list of studies currently happening at BluePearl hospitals. There, you'll find more information about qualifications.
L65: 
L66: For questions about specific studies, you can also reach out to the study contact listed to discuss your pet’s eligibility.
L67: 
L68: How does BluePearl ensure studies are conducted safely and ethically?
L69: Enrollment in a clinical study is always up to the pet owner and our informed consent process for clinical studies ensures that owners are fully aware of the study's objectives, any potential risks and study requirements before they agree to allow their pets to participate. Owners always sign a written consent form before their pet is enrolled in a study.
L70: As part of the Mars Veterinary Health family of brands, BluePearl Science strictly adheres to the Mars Policy on Clinical Studies. Clinical studies at BluePearl undergo a rigorous review process to ensure the highest medical and ethical care standards for all pets and their owners.
L71: This process is conducted by our Veterinary Clinical Studies Committee (VCSC), comprised of individuals with specific expertise in clinical medicine and surgery, clinical and basic research, animal welfare and regulatory issues, the human-animal bond and social work, and members of the community not affiliated with BluePearl or Mars.
L72: I’m interested in sponsoring or collaborating on a clinical study. How can I work with BluePearl hospitals?
L73: BluePearl Science leverages one of the world’s largest private providers of specialty and emergency veterinary care to advance new and exciting diagnostics and treatments for our veterinary patients. We coordinate clinical studies across a national network of 100+ hospitals. BluePearl Science carries out collaborative research only with institutions that comply with our animal welfare and ethical standards, and we welcome the opportunity to discuss your upcoming project.
L74: Contact us at 【8†[email protected]】.
L75: ### Current canine clinical studies:
L76: 
L77: 【9†A New Treatment for Dogs with Chronic Inflammatory Enteropathy】
L78: Locations: Langhorne, PA
L79: Purpose: This study will evaluate the efficacy and safety of a new treatment versus placebo for chronic inflammatory enteropathy (previously known as inflammatory bowel disease) in dogs.
L80: 【10†Medial Elbow Replacement Surgery】
L81: Locations: Golden Valley, MN; Arden Hills, MN
L82: Purpose: This clinical evaluation study is validating the surgical technique and assessing the safety and efficacy of the medial elbow replacement surgery.
L83: 
L84: 【11†Treatment for Canine Hemangiosarcoma (HSA) of the Spleen】
L85: Locations: Kirkland, WA; Tacoma, WA
L86: Purpose: To evaluate the efficacy of a chemotherapy protocol for the treatment of canine hemangiosarcoma of the spleen.
L87: 【12†Canine Atopic Dermatitis】
L88: Locations: Malvern, PA; Midvale, UT; Reno, NV; Ft. Lauderdale, FL
L89: Purpose: This study will evaluate the efficacy of a new treatment for canine atopic dermatitis.
L90: 
L91: 【13†Mars Petcare Biobank】
L92: Locations: Clearwater, FL; Brandon, FL; Tampa, FL
L93: Purpose: By studying a pet’s health throughout its life, scientists will seek to identify potential signs of disease as well as new ways to help prevent or even predict illness.
L94: ### Current feline clinical studies:
L95: 
L96: 【13†Mars Petcare Biobank】
L97: Location: Clearwater, FL, Brandon, FL and Tampa, FL
L98: Purpose: By studying a pet’s health throughout its life, scientists will seek to identify potential signs of disease as well as new ways to help prevent or even predict illness.
L99: 
L100: 【14†The HALT Study for Cats】
L101: Location: Reno, NV
L102: Purpose: This study will investigate the efficacy of a new medication for the treatment of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) in cats.
L103:

L106: 
L107: For more information about BluePearl Science, email 【16†[email protected]】.

L39: 【11†Image: Masyr 2】 Dr. Masyr and a patient with lymphoma.
L40: 
L41: Species: Dog
L42: 
L43: Area of Study: Medical Oncology
L44: Purpose of Study: The purpose of this study is to provide a direct comparison between the outcomes for dogs with peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL) treated with CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. The findings of this study could help veterinarians understand if one protocol is truly superior to the other for dogs with PTCL.
L45: 
L46: In this study, your dog will be randomly selected to receive either CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. At each visit, their lymph node size, blood work, and overall wellbeing will be assessed.
L47: Timeline: Both protocols involve treatments every 7–14 days and take 4-6 months to complete. Following protocol completion, your pet will return once monthly to assess remission status.
L48: 
L49: Eligibility: Your dog may qualify if:
L50:   * Confirmed peripheral T cell lymphoma diagnosis via cytology or histopathology
L51:     * No indolent forms of lymphoma, such as T zone lymphoma
L52:     * Cutaneous lymphoma will not be included
L53:   * No prior chemotherapy or radiation therapy for lymphoma. It is preferred that patients are not started on steroids in advance of enrollment. However, if deemed by the overseeing clinician, patients can still be enrolled on steroids for up to 10 days.
L54:   * No major lab work abnormalities that prevent chemotherapy administration
L55:   * No evidence of dilated cardiomyopathy, ventricular arrhythmia, or liver failure
L56: ## T Cell Diagnostic Testing
L57: 
L58: A diagnosis of T cell lymphoma can be made using one or more of the following tests:
L59: 
L60:   * Immunocytochemistry (ICC)*
L61:   * Immunohistochemistry (IHC)*
L62:   * PCR for antigen receptor rearrangements (PARR)*
L63:   * Flow cytometry
L64: 
L65: *Available through the 【12†MSU Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory†vdl.msu.edu】
L66: 
L67: Client Benefits: This is a partially funded trial.
L68:   * A test must be conducted to confirm the T cell lymphoma diagnosis in study participants. T cell diagnostic testing can be conducted at MSU or through clients’ primary care veterinarians. Diagnostic testing at MSU costs approximately $250. For dogs accepted to the study, the cost will be reimbursed by an account credit at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center at trial completion (either when the protocol is completed or the patient develops progressive disease).
L69:   * Initial evaluation appointments will be charged. For dogs accepted to the study, recheck exams during clinical trial appointments will be free of cost ($60 value per visit). Costs associated with blood work and treatment will remain the responsibility of the client (with the exception described below).
L70:   * Dogs will receive the first dose of doxorubicin (for those assigned to the CHOP protocol) or lomustine (for those assigned to the LOPP protocol) free of cost. First-dose administrative and blood work fees also will be free of cost.
L71:   * Clients are financially responsible for all treatments and diagnostics that are unrelated to the study.
L72: Client Responsibilities:
L73:   * To administer prednisone, chemotherapy, or supplemental medications as prescribed by the attending veterinarian.
L74:   * To comply with the visit schedule outlined by study investigators
L75:   * To report any abnormal behavior or signs of illness to study investigators.
L76:   * To contact study investigators if your dog is evaluated by any other veterinarians during the course of the study.
L77:   * To inform study investigators of any non-study-related veterinary treatments recommended for your dog during the course of the study.
L78: Contact Information: Please feel free to contact our Medical Oncology Team at (517) 353-5420 or cvm.oncoinfo@msu.edu to refer a patient or for any additional information. Referring veterinarian and client calls are welcome.
L79: 
L80: Practitioners of interest: Primary care and specialty clinics, especially oncology specialties, in Michigan, Indiana, Ohio, Canada, and surrounding areas.

L54: #### ​Purpose of Study
L55: Immunotherapy, engaging the power of the immune system against cancer, has become a standard part of oncology care. One such approach utilizes the STimulator of INterferon Genes (STING) pathway. Our colleagues at University of Michigan, led by Dr. James Moon, have developed a drug that activates the STING pathway. This drug, called CMP-002, has been shown to combat cancer in a laboratory setting, with and without the use of another modulator of immune system, PD-1 blockade.
L56: This success prompted a collaboration with Michigan State University College of Veterinary Medicine as we hope to contribute to efforts that can help veterinary oncology patients and humans alike. Our initial studies, led by Dr. Vilma Yuzbasiyan-Gurkan at MSU, established the dose range tolerated in healthy dogs.
L57: The purpose of this study is to confirm the best dose of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade for tumor-bearing dogs. CMP-002 has already been tested in healthy dogs. It is not uncommon for patients with cancer to process drugs differently, which is why we intend to confirm the best dose for tumor-bearing dogs. The findings of this study will then be used in future studies assessing the anti-cancer properties of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade.
L58: #### Eligibility Criteria
L59:   * Inclusion criteria:
L60:     * Confirmed diagnosis of soft tissue sarcoma, lymphoma, osteosarcoma, histiocytic sarcoma, or malignant melanoma via cytology or histopathology.
L61:     * Visible tumor at the time of enrollment.
L62:     * Adequate organ function indicated by standard laboratory tests.
L63:     * Minimum weight requirement of 5 kg (11 lbs).
L64:   * Exclusion criteria:
L65:     * Prior anti-cancer treatment, including steroids, within 7 days.
L66:     * Indolent forms of lymphoma, such as T zone lymphoma.
L67:     * Expected survival < 4 weeks with treatment.
L68: #### Eligibility Diagnostics
L69: 
L70: Prior to study entry, pet owners will be charged an initial consultation fee and be financially responsible and required to have the following diagnostics performed in their dog:
L71: 
L72:   1. Diagnosis of select tumor type, if not already documented
L73:   2. Screening blood work and urinalysis, if not performed within 7 days
L74: #### Treatment
L75: The first group of patients (6–9 dogs) will receive CMP-002 alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the CMP-002 infusion. They will then be observed overnight and blood samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will visit their primary veterinarians one week later for blood sampling. Three weeks after the first treatment, the dogs will return to the MSU Veterinary Medical Center for a second infusion.
L76: Depending on previous response, they may be hospitalized again or sent home the same day. If tolerated, these treatments can be repeated every 3 weeks for a set number of cycles. Tumor biopsy samples may be collected at various timepoints.
L77: The second group of dogs (6–9 dogs) will receive CMP-002 with PD-1 blockade. Their tumor will measured and they will receive the CMP-002 infusion. They will then be observed overnight and blood samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return one week later for tumor measurements, blood sampling, and anti-PD-1 infusion. Three weeks after the first treatment, the dogs will return to the MSU Veterinary Medical Center for a second CMP-002 infusion.
L78: Depending on previous response, they may be hospitalized again or sent home the same day. If tolerated, these treatments can be repeated every 3 weeks for a set number of cycles. Tumor biopsy samples may be collected at various timepoints.
L79: #### Compensation
L80:   * This is a funded trial. All tests and treatments associated with the trial will be covered once a dog is enrolled.
L81:   * Complications associated with the trial will be covered. Clients are financially responsible for all treatments and diagnostics that are unrelated to the trial. Association between complications and trial treatment will be determined by the overseeing clinician and investigators.
L82:   * Initial evaluation appointments will be charged. For dogs accepted to the study, recheck exams during clinical trial appointments will be free of cost ($60 value per visit).
L83:   * CMP-002 (and PD-1 blockade, if included) treatment will be administered free of cost. Hospitalization immediately after CMP-002 administration and associated treatments will be free of cost. Blood sampling and tumor biopsies associated with the trial will be free of cost.
L84:   * One week after CMP-002, blood work will be needed. If performed at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center, the cost will be covered by the trial. If performed through your local veterinarian, you will be reimbursed up to $99 per test.
L85: Note: Test and treatments associated with the trial are covered for enrolled dogs. This does not include any surgical procedures.
L86: #### Contact Information
L87: 
L88: Please feel free to contact our Medical Oncology Team at (517) 353-5420 or cvm.oncoinfo@msu.edu to refer a patient or for any additional information. Referring veterinarian and client calls are welcome.
